Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Maid
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 51

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Raj is a 52-year-old man who came to therapy at the urging of his daughter, Priya, after months of what he called "bad spells." He had stopped leaving his apartment except for work, and even then he moved through his shifts as a cleaner for a private home in a kind of trance, his hands doing the motions while his mind was somewhere else. He knew something had broken inside him the day the guest fell, and it had never come back together.

The accident had happened eighteen months earlier, when Raj was still working at a downtown hotel. He had been pushing a heavy linen cart through the lobby, his phone buzzing in his pocket with a call from his ex-wife about a missed alimony payment. He glanced down at the screen, just for a second, and when he looked up the guest had stepped backward directly into the cart’s metal handle. The impact caught the man behind the knee, his legs buckled, and he went down hard, his head hitting the marble floor with a sound Raj still heard in his sleep. A fractured skull, a subdural hematoma, three weeks in intensive care. The guest recovered enough to walk with a cane, but the hotel settled the lawsuit, and Raj was fired that same week.

What stayed with Raj were not the legal consequences or the lost job. What stayed with him were the seconds themselves—each one a still image he could flip through in his mind like a deck of cards: the guest’s surprised face, the exact angle of the cart, the phone still buzzing in his pocket. He could not run the memory as a continuous film; it came in fragments, each one equally vivid and equally unbearable. And it came without warning. A stack of laundry in a hallway, the squeak of a cart’s wheel, the ringtone of his daughter’s phone—any of these could drop him right back into the lobby, his chest tight, his hands shaking, his jaw clenched with a rage so hot it frightened him. He was not angry at the guest, or at the hotel. He was angry at himself, at his own carelessness, at the fact that he had looked at a phone when he should have been looking at the world. The rage hit him every time he remembered, and he remembered all the time.

Raj had always thought of himself as a careful man. He took pride in his work, in the neat lines of a freshly made bed, the streak-free shine of a window. The accident had shown him something different: that he could be careless, that he could hurt someone without meaning to, that his own hands could become instruments of harm. The thought went against everything he believed about himself, and it hollowed out the meaning of everything he did. What was the point of folding sheets perfectly when the same hands had put a man in a hospital bed? He had stopped calling friends, stopped visiting his brother, stopped watching the cricket matches he used to love. None of it mattered anymore.

The private home where he now worked was a deliberate choice. It had fewer people, fewer carts, fewer triggers. But the avoidance had cost him: he made half of what he used to, he could barely afford his rent, and he lived in constant fear that he would somehow cause harm again. He moved slowly through the house, checking every corner, holding cleaning bottles with two hands as if they were weapons. His daughter told him he was not the same father who used to joke with her at the dinner table. He knew she was right.

What finally brought Raj to seek help was a moment last week, when he heard the homeowner’s grandson trip on a rug and cry out. The sound—the thud of a fall—sent Raj into a full flashback in the middle of the kitchen. He had stood frozen, a dishrag in his hand, seeing the lobby marble, hearing the crack, feeling the rage and shame surge up his throat. He could not keep living this way. He came to therapy not because he believed it would fix him, but because he was tired of being a man he did not recognise. What he feared most, he said, was that he would never forgive himself. What he hoped for, quietly, was that his daughter might one day see him smile again.
